title: Koko Eating Bananas
summary: Each hour Koko eats up to k bananas from one pile. Return the smallest k that lets her finish every pile within h hours.
statement:
There are `piles.length` piles of bananas; pile `i` has `piles[i]` bananas. Koko picks an eating speed `k` (bananas per hour). Each hour she picks one pile and eats `k` bananas from it; if the pile has fewer than `k`, she finishes it and does not start another pile that hour.

Return the smallest integer `k` that lets her eat every banana within `h` hours.
hints: If speed k works, any faster speed also works. That monotonic "works / doesn't work" shape is a cue for binary search on the answer.
For a given k, the hours needed are the sum of ceil(piles[i] / k). Binary-search k between 1 and max(piles).
Compute ceil as (p + k − 1) / k and keep the hour total in a long. Find the smallest k with hours ≤ h.
explain: At speed 4 the piles take 1, 2, 2 and 3 hours (each pile rounds up), 8 hours in total, which fits `h = 8`. At speed 3 they take 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 hours, too many. So the slowest speed that works is 4.

title: Find the Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold
summary: Divide every value by d, rounding up, and add the results. Return the smallest positive d that keeps the sum at most threshold.
statement:
Choose a positive integer divisor `d`. Divide every value of `nums` by `d`, rounding each result up, and add them together.

Return the smallest `d` for which that sum is at most `threshold`. An answer always exists.
hints: A larger divisor never increases the sum. So the condition "sum ≤ threshold" flips from false to true exactly once as d grows.
Binary-search d between 1 and max(nums), computing the rounded-up sum for each candidate.
Look for the smallest d that satisfies the condition: when it holds, set hi = mid; otherwise lo = mid + 1.
explain: Dividing by 5 and rounding up gives 1, 1, 1 and 2, which sum to 5 ≤ 6. Dividing by 4 gives 1, 1, 2 and 3, summing to 7, which is over the threshold. So the smallest divisor that works is 5.

title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
summary: Packages must ship in the given order, filling the ship each day without exceeding its capacity. Return the smallest capacity that ships everything within days days.
statement:
Packages with weights `weights[i]` must be shipped in the given order. Each day the ship is loaded with packages in order until adding the next one would exceed its capacity; then it sails, and the remaining packages wait for the next day.

Return the smallest ship capacity that ships every package within `days` days.
hints: The capacity must be at least the heaviest package and is never more than the total weight.
For a candidate capacity, simulate greedily: fill each day until the next package does not fit, and count the days.
Binary-search the smallest capacity whose day count is ≤ days.
explain: With capacity 15 the days are `[1,2,3,4,5]`, `[6,7]`, `[8]`, `[9]` and `[10]`: 5 days, in order, none over 15. With capacity 14 the same greedy loading needs 6 days. So 15 is the smallest capacity that ships everything within 5 days.

title: Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets
summary: Flower i blooms on bloomDay[i]. A bouquet needs k adjacent bloomed flowers. Return the fewest days to make m bouquets, or -1 if impossible.
statement:
Flower `i` blooms on day `bloomDay[i]` and stays bloomed. To make a bouquet you need `k` adjacent flowers that have all bloomed, and each flower can be used in only one bouquet.

Return the minimum number of days you must wait to be able to make `m` bouquets, or `-1` if it can never be done.
hints: If m × k is more than the number of flowers, the answer is −1 immediately (compute it as a long).
Waiting longer never hurts, so binary-search the day between min(bloomDay) and max(bloomDay).
To test a day, scan left to right counting bloomed flowers in a row; every time the run reaches k, make a bouquet and reset the run.
explain: Each bouquet needs `k = 1` flower. By day 3 the flowers blooming on days 1, 3 and 2 are open, enough for 3 bouquets. On day 2 only two flowers are open. So the answer is day 3.

title: Minimum Time to Complete Trips
summary: Bus i takes time[i] for one trip and can repeat trips back to back; buses run in parallel. Return the least time for all buses together to finish at least totalTrips trips.
statement:
Bus `i` needs `time[i]` units of time for one trip and can start its next trip as soon as it finishes. All buses run at the same time, independently.

Return the minimum time needed for the buses together to complete at least `totalTrips` trips.
hints: By time T, bus i has completed T / time[i] trips (integer division).
The total trips grow as T grows, so binary-search the smallest T with sum(T / time[i]) ≥ totalTrips.
The upper bound is min(time) × totalTrips, which needs a long. Stop summing early once you reach totalTrips to avoid overflow.
explain: In 3 units of time the buses finish 3 ÷ 1 = 3, 3 ÷ 2 = 1 and 3 ÷ 3 = 1 trips (rounded down), 5 in total. In 2 units they finish only 2 + 1 + 0 = 3 trips. So the minimum time is 3.

title: Magnetic Force Between Two Balls
summary: Place m balls into baskets at the given positions to maximise the smallest distance between any two balls. Return that distance.
statement:
There are baskets at the distinct positions in `position`. Place `m` balls into baskets, at most one ball per basket, so that the smallest distance between any two balls is as large as possible.

Return that largest possible minimum distance.
hints: Sort the positions. Then ask: can I place m balls so every two are at least d apart?
Check d greedily: put a ball in the first basket, then in the next basket at least d further, and so on. Count how many fit.
If m balls fit for d, they also fit for any smaller d. Binary-search the largest d that works.
explain: Placing the 3 balls at positions 1, 4 and 7 makes the closest pair 3 apart. A minimum gap of 4 is impossible: after 1 the next free position at least 4 away is 7, and nothing fits after it. So the largest possible minimum force is 3.

title: Split Array Largest Sum
summary: Split the array into k non-empty contiguous parts so the largest part sum is as small as possible. Return that sum.
statement:
Split `nums` into `k` non-empty contiguous parts. Of all ways to do it, choose the one in which the largest part sum is as small as possible, and return that largest sum.

The parts keep the original order and together cover every element exactly once. Among all ways of making exactly `k` parts, look at each split's largest part sum and return the smallest such value.
hints: Flip the question: given a limit L, can you split nums into at most k parts with each part sum ≤ L?
Check L greedily: keep adding to the current part until the next value would exceed L, then start a new part. Count the parts.
Binary-search L between max(nums) and sum(nums), using long sums. The smallest L that needs ≤ k parts is the answer.
explain: Splitting into `[7,2,5]` and `[10,8]` gives sums 14 and 18, so the largest part is 18. Every other split into 2 parts has a larger maximum (for example `[7,2,5,10] | [8]` has 24), so the answer is 18.
